sentences.text: Here are two hundred providers, and a secret.
Six of them truly differ from the reference: three worse, three better. The other 194 are, in truth, identical.
And here are their ratios, sorted from highest to lowest. A league table.
Can you pick out the six?
Take the three at the top and the three at the bottom, and you would be right about two. The other four are identical providers, small ones, having a lucky or an unlucky year.
A league table cannot tell luck from difference. We need a picture that can.
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: the funnel.
Start with Dune's pile from Episode 13: what luck allows, for a clinic like the reference with Dune's patients.
Divide every count by the 4.8 expected, and the pile sits on the ratio scale, centred on 1.
Keep the stretch that holds 95% of it: from 0.38 to 1.62.
Stand that band upright. A ratio inside it is unremarkable for Dune.
How wide the band is depends on how much a clinic can tell us. Call that its precision. Dune's is 10.
Birch has more to go on: a precision of 39, and a narrower band, from 0.69 to 1.31.
Now do that at every precision, and join the edges.
Wide on the left, where clinics tell us little. Narrow on the right. A funnel.
Place the cast. Dune, Cedar and Birch sit inside. Alder, at 1.62, is outside.
Outside the funnel means flagged, by last episode's bell-curve test. It is the same calculation, drawn.
And Elm, far to the left. At Elm's precision the lower edge is below zero. No count, not even none, could flag so small a clinic as better than the reference.
Now the two hundred from the start. Of the 194 identical providers, 13 fall outside the funnel, by luck alone.
That is what a 5% line means. Draw the crowd again and again, and on average 5% of them land outside.
And the six who truly differ? The funnel catches three.
It misses both of the small ones, with 37 patients each. And it misses a better-than-reference provider with 105: a low count is harder to prove than a high one.
So a dot outside is not a verdict, and a dot inside is not an acquittal. Inside means consistent with the reference, not equal to it.
Why put precision along the bottom, and not the number of patients?
Take two providers with 100 patients each. One treats patients whose risk is near 5%; the other, near 40%.
Their precisions are 5 and 67. The same size, at opposite ends of the funnel.
In our crowd, providers of about a hundred patients have precisions from 19 to 74.
One companion picture. Sort the providers by ratio, and give each one its interval from Episode 13.
The funnel shows how much each provider can tell us. The caterpillar shows the order, and how little the order can be trusted.
A footnote on the funnel. With the exact test, each provider has limits of its own, stepping between whole counts. The smooth curve is a guide to them.
One last turn of a knob. Until now, all but six of our providers were identical. Let them truly differ a little, as real providers do.
Now a quarter of the dots are outside the funnel.
Is each of them an outlier? Or is the funnel too narrow for a world in which everyone differs? Hold that question. It has an episode of its own.
Let's gather it up.
Up the side, the ratio. Along the bottom, precision: how much a provider can tell us.
The funnel is what luck allows at each precision. Outside it means flagged.
And dots on the left are not worse providers. They are quieter ones.
Every picture in this act has leaned on something we have not yet questioned: the risk model itself.
Next time: can we trust it?
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
